source_text:
Εἶπόν σοι, φησίν, ὅτι τὰ κτίσματα τοῦ θεοῦ διπλᾶ ἐστι: καὶ γὰρ ἡ ἐγκράτεια διπλῆ ἐστιν. ἐπί τινων γὰρ δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, ἐπί τινων δὲ οὐ δεῖ:
Γνώρισόν μοι, φημί, κύριε, ἐπὶ τίνων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, ἐπὶ τίνων δὲ οὐ δεῖ. Ἄκουε, φησί. τὸ πονηρὸν ἐγκρατεύου καὶ μὴ ποίει αὐτό: τὸ δὲ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ἐγκρατεύου, ἀλλὰ ποίει αὐτὸ. ἐὰν γὰρ ἐγκρατεύσῃ τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ποιεῖν, ἁμαρτίαν μεγάλην ἐργάζῃ: ἐὰν δὲ ἐγκρατεύσῃ τὸ πονηρὸν μὴ ποιεῖν, δικαιοσύνην μεγάλην ἐργάζῃ. ἐγκράτευσαι οὖν ἀπὸ πονηρίας πάσης ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθόν.
Ποταπαί, φημί, κύριε, εἰσὶν αἱ πονηρίαι, ἀφ̓ ὧν ἡμᾶς δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι; Ἄκουε, φησίν: ἀπὸ μοιχείας καὶ πορνείας, ἀπὸ μεθύσματος ἀνομίας, ἀπὸ τρυφῆς πονηρᾶς, ἀπὸ ἐδεσμάτων πολλῶν καὶ πολυτελείας πλούτου καὶ καυχήσεως καὶ ὑψηλοφροσύνης καὶ ὑπερηφανίας καὶ ἀπὸ ψεύσματος καὶ καταλαλιᾶς καὶ ὑποκρίσεως, μνησικακίας καὶ πάσης βλασφημίας.
ταῦτα τὰ ἔργα πάντων πονηρότατά εἰσιν ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἀπὸ τούτων οὖν τῶν ἔργων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ θεοῦ: ὁ γὰρ μὴ ἐγκρατευόμενος ἀπὸ τούτων οὐ δύναται ζῆσαι τῷ θεῷ. ἄκουε οὖν καὶ τὰ ἀκόλουθα τούτων,
Ἔτι γάρ, φημί, κύριε, πονηρὰ ἔργα ἐστί; Καί γε πολλά, φησίν, ἔστιν, ἀφ̓ ὧν δεῖ τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι: κλέμμα, ψεῦδος, ἀποστέρησις, ψευδομαρτυρία, πλεονεξία, ἐπιθυμία πονηρά, ἀπάτη, κενοδοξία, ἀλαζονεία καὶ ὅσα τούτοις ὅμοιά εἰσιν.
οὐ δοκεῖ σοι ταῦτα πονηρὰ εἶναι; καὶ λίαν πονηρά, φημί, τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ. τούτων πάντων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν δουλεύοντα τῷ θεῷ. ἐγκράτευσαι οὖν ἀπὸ πάντων τούτων, ἵνα ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐγγραφήσῃ μετὰ τῶν ἐγκρατευομένων αὐτά. ὧν μὲν οὖν δεῖ σε ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, ταῦτά ἐστιν.
ἃ δὲ δεῖ σε μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, φησίν, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖν, ἄκουε. τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ἐγκρατεύου, ἀλλὰ ποίει αὐτό.
Καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν μοι, φημί, κύριε, δήλωσον τὴν δύναμιν, ἵνα πορευθῶ ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ δουλεύσω αὐτοῖς, ἵνα ἐργασάμενος αὐτὰ δυνηθῶ σωθῆναι. Ἄκουε, φησί, καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὰ ἔργα, ἅ σε δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι.
πρῶτον πάντων πίστις, φόβος κυρίου, ἀγάπη, ὁμόνοια, ῥήματα δικαιοσύνης, ἀλήθεια, ὑπομονή: τούτων ἀγαθώτερον οὐδέν ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ταῦτα ἐάν τις φυλάσσῃ καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύηται ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, μακάριος γίνεται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ.
εἶτα τούτων τὰ ἀκόλουθα ἄκουσον: χήραις ὑπηρετεῖν, ὀρφανοὺς καὶ ὑστερουμένους ἐπισκέπτεσθαι, ἐξ ἀναγκῶν λυτροῦσθαι τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ, φιλόξενον εἶναι ʽἐν γὰρ τῇ φιλοξενίᾳ εὑρίσκεται ἀγαθοποίησίς ποτἐ, μηδενὶ ἀντιτάσσεσθαι, ἡσύχιον εἶναι, ἐνδεέστερον γίνεσθαι πάντων ἀνθρώπων, πρεσβύτας σέβεσθαι, δικαιοσύνην ἀσκεῖν, ἀδελφότητα συντηρεῖν, ὕβριν ὑποφέρειν, μακρόθυμον εἶναι, μνησικακίαν μὴ ἔχειν, κάμνοντας τῇ φυχῇ παρακαλεῖν, ἐσκανδαλισμένους ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως μὴ ἀποβάλλεσθαι, ἀλλ’ ἐπιστρέφειν καὶ εὐθύμους ποιεῖν, ἁμαρτάνοντας νουθετεῖν, χρεώστας μὴ θλίβειν καὶ ἐνδεεῖς, καὶ εἴ τινα τούτοις ὅμοιά ἐστι.
δοκεῖ σοι, φησί, ταῦτα ἀγαθὰ εἶναι; Τί γάρ, φημί, κύριε, τούτων ἀγαθώτερον; Πορεύου οὖν, φησίν, ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύου ἀπ’ αὐτῶν, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ:
φύλασσε οὖν τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην: ἐὰν τὸ ἀγαθὸν ποιῇς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύσῃ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ, ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ οἱ οὕτω ποιοῦντες. καὶ πάλιν ἐὰν τὸ πονηρὸν μὴ ποιῇς καὶ ἐγκρατεύσῃ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ, ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ, ὅσοι ἐὰν ταύτας τὰς ἐντολὰς φυλάξωσι καὶ πορευθῶσιν ἐν αὐταῖς.
thought_title: Two kinds of self-control: from evil, not from good
orientation: The Shepherd gives Hermas the eighth commandment, on self-control. Self-control here means holding back: hold back from evil, but never hold back from good.
pass_a_gloss: I told you, he says, that the creatures of God are double; for also self-control is double. For over some things one must exercise self-control, but over some things one must not. Make known to me, I say, sir, over what things one must exercise self-control, and over what things one must not. Listen, he says. Exercise self-control over the evil thing and do not do it; but do not exercise self-control over the good thing, but do it. For if you exercise self-control so as not to do the good, you work a great sin; but if you exercise self-control so as not to do the evil, you work a great righteousness. Exercise self-control therefore from all evil, working the good. What kinds, I say, sir, are the evils, from which we must exercise self-control? Listen, he says: from adultery and fornication, from lawless drunkenness, from evil luxury, from many foods and from extravagance of wealth and from boasting and from arrogance and from pride and from lying and from slander and from hypocrisy, from bearing of grudges and from all blasphemy. These works are the most evil of all in the life of men. From these works therefore the servant of God must exercise self-control; for the one who does not exercise self-control from these cannot live to God. Listen therefore also to the things that follow these. Are there still, I say, sir, evil works? Yes indeed many, he says, there are, from which the servant of God must exercise self-control: theft, lying, robbery, false witness, greed, evil desire, deceit, vainglory, boastfulness and as many things as are like these. Does it not seem to you that these are evil? Very evil indeed, I say, for the servants of God. From all these the one who serves God must exercise self-control. Exercise self-control therefore from all these, in order that you may live to God and may be enrolled with those who exercise self-control over them. The things therefore from which you must exercise self-control are these. But the things over which you must not exercise self-control, he says, but do them, listen. Do not exercise self-control over the good, but do it. And of the good things, I say, sir, show me the power, in order that I may walk in them and serve them, in order that having worked them I may be able to be saved. Listen, he says, also to the works of the good things, which you must work and not exercise self-control over. First of all faith, fear of the Lord, love, concord, words of righteousness, truth, patience; than these nothing is better in the life of men. If anyone guards these and does not exercise self-control from them, he becomes blessed in his life. Then listen to the things that follow these: to serve widows, to visit orphans and the destitute, to redeem the servants of God from necessities, to be hospitable (for in hospitality good-doing is found at some time), to oppose no one, to be quiet, to become needier than all men, to reverence elders, to practice righteousness, to preserve brotherhood, to endure insolence, to be patient, not to have bearing of grudges, to comfort those who are weary in soul, not to cast away those who have been made to stumble from the faith, but to turn them back and make them cheerful, to admonish those who sin, not to oppress debtors and the needy, and if there are any things like these. Does it seem to you, he says, that these are good? What indeed, I say, sir, is better than these? Walk therefore, he says, in them and do not exercise self-control from them, and you will live to God. Guard therefore this commandment: if you do the good and do not exercise self-control from it, you will live to God, and all will live to God who do thus. And again if you do not do the evil and exercise self-control from it, you will live to God, and all will live to God, as many as guard these commandments and walk in them.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term; must be used consistently for this key virtue.
Verbal form of the glossary term; keeps the connection to self-control explicit.

choices.term: τὰ κτίσματα τοῦ θεοῦ διπλᾶ ἐστι
choices.english: the creatures of God are double
choices.why: Literal rendering preserves the Shepherd's opening claim that creation is twofold, which frames the whole argument.
rejected: the created things of God are of two kinds

choices.why: Consistent with the previous section's rendering of this phrase; keeps the dative force.

choices.english: be enrolled with those who exercise self-control
choices.why: The verb suggests being written into a register; 'enrolled' captures the image of being listed among the self-controlled.
Literal comparative; the Shepherd calls for humility that places oneself below others in need.

pass_b_english: “I told you,” the Shepherd said, “that the things God has created are twofold. Self-control is twofold as well. For there are some things from which we must hold back, and some from which we must not.”

“Make known to me, sir,” I said, “from what things we must hold back, and from what things we must not.” “Listen,” he said. “Hold back from evil, and do not do it. But do not hold back from good. Do it. For if you hold back from doing good, you commit a great sin. But if you hold back from doing evil, you do a great act of righteousness. So hold back from all wickedness, and do what is good.”

“Sir,” I said, “what kinds of wickedness must we hold back from?” “Listen,” he said. “From adultery and sexual immorality. From lawless drunkenness. From wicked luxury. From much food, and the extravagance of wealth, and boasting, and haughtiness, and pride. From lying and slander and hypocrisy, from bearing grudges, and from all blasphemy.
“These deeds are the most evil of all in human life. So the servant of God must hold back from these deeds. For whoever does not hold back from them cannot live to God. Now hear what follows them.”

“Sir,” I said, “are there still more evil deeds?” “Yes, many more,” he said, “from which the servant of God must hold back: theft, falsehood, fraud, false witness, greed, evil desire, deceit, conceit, boastfulness, and everything like these.

“Do you not think these are evil?” “Very evil indeed,” I said, “for the servants of God.” “From all of these,” he said, “the one who serves God must hold back. So hold back from all of them, so that you may live to God and be enrolled among those who hold back from them. These, then, are the things from which you must hold back.
“Now hear,” he said, “the things from which you must not hold back, but which you must do. Do not hold back from good. Do it.”

“Sir,” I said, “show me the power of the good things as well, so that I may walk in them and serve them, and by doing them can be saved.” “Then hear,” he said, “the works of goodness too, which you must do, and from which you must not hold back.

“First of all: faith, fear of the Lord, love, harmony, words of righteousness, truth, endurance. Nothing in human life is better than these. If anyone keeps them and does not hold back from them, he becomes blessed in his life.

“Then hear what follows these: to serve widows, to visit orphans and those in need, to rescue the servants of God from hardship, and to be hospitable, for in hospitality good is sometimes done. To oppose no one, to be quiet, to be poorer than everyone else. To respect the aged, to practice righteousness, to preserve brotherhood, to bear insult, to be patient, to hold no grudge. To comfort those who are weary in soul. Not to cast off those who have stumbled from the faith, but to turn them back and put them in good heart. To admonish sinners, not to press hard on debtors or the needy, and whatever else is like these.
“Do these seem good to you?” he said. “Sir,” I said, “what could be better than these?” “Then walk in them,” he said, “and do not hold back from them, and you will live to God.

“So keep this commandment. If you do good and do not hold back from it, you will live to God, and all who do the same will live to God. And again, if you do not do evil, but hold back from it, you will live to God. And all will live to God who keep these commandments and walk in them.”

problems.why: Same Greek virtue (enkrateia) rendered as 'self-control' and 'Self-Control' (personified), but 'self-willed' in section 26 translates different Greek word (authades) yet may confuse readers tracking virtues.
problems.fix: Add note that 'self-willed' is different Greek word, not same virtue.

problems.why: Three overlapping terms for saved community used inconsistently; reader cannot tell if these are identical groups or distinct categories.
problems.fix: Clarify in intro whether these are synonyms or distinct groups in Hermas's theology.

problems.quote: to become needier than all men
problems.why: Context lists virtues, but 'needier' seems like vice; Greek ptōchoteros may mean 'poor in spirit' or 'humble,' not literally poorer.
problems.fix: Translate as 'more humble' or 'poorer in spirit' to match virtue list context.

edits.old: to become needier than all men
edits.new: to become poorer in spirit than all men

fixed: The glossary note about 'self-willed' is a note for the glossary, not an edit to the English text; no change made to the translation.
The glossary note about 'the elect' is a note for the glossary, not an edit to the English text; no change made to the translation.

The Greek πτωχότερος (ptōchoteros) in this virtue list context means 'poorer in spirit' or 'more humble,' not literally poorer in material goods; changed 'needier' to 'poorer in spirit' to match the virtue list.
